extracted.intended_audience: theologians, seminary students, clergy, and scholars of Catholic doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Catholic teaching (esp. Council of Trent and scholastic sources) on grace, faith, baptism, contrition, and the nature and causes of justification. The page collects canons, scriptural citations, and theological commentary setting doctrinal requirements and distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith as the beginning and foundation of salvation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Fides est humanae salutis initium, fundamentum et radix omnis iustificationis.” (Council of Trent, Sess. VI, cap. 8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faith is presented as the necessary initiating principle of human salvation; the text also explains that faith is received 'ex auditu' when awakened and aided by divine grace (Sess. VI, cap. 6) which moves the will freely to God. Several patristic and scholastic citations support this claim (Heb. XI, 6; St. Augustine, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of a bare fiducial faith (faith as mere trust)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sess. VI, can. 12 condemns the view that justifying faith is nothing other than trust in divine mercy or mere fiducial trust alone: such a reduction is anathematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canonical condemnation makes plain that faith cannot be understood as mere confidence without the content and effects (i.e., it must be the faith taught by divine revelation and inseparable from certain dispositions); the Council and subsequent commentators distinguish proper justifying faith from a minimal trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of sola fide (faith alone as sufficient for justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sess. VI, can. 9 and related canons anathematize the claim that men are justified by faith alone so that nothing else cooperates to obtain justification, or that they are prepared by their own will alone for justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly stresses that justification involves more than imputed faith alone; it includes sanctification and interior renewal and presupposes divine grace and the infusion of charity (Sess. VI, cap. 7 and can. 11, can. 10, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of certain explicit articles of faith for those bound by precept
rubrics_metrics.description: St. Thomas (2a 2ae, qu. 2, art. 7) and the page assert that after the revelation of grace certain mysteries (especially those solemnly proposed by the Church, e.g., articles of the Incarnation) must be explicitly believed by those subject to the precept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some subtleties of assent may vary by state and office, the Council and theologians require explicit belief in publicly proposed mysteries for those obligated under ecclesiastical precept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Missionary duty to explain necessary mysteries to capable adults
rubrics_metrics.description: A missionary is bound to explain the mysteries necessary by the necessity of the means (e.g., Trinity and Incarnation) to an adult who is not entirely incapacitated (Prop. Damn. ab Innocentio XI, prop. 64).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets an operative pastoral/ministerial obligation: those who can understand must be taught the essential revealed truths that are necessary mediating causes of salvation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrition required for remission of mortal sin; degrees of contrition
rubrics_metrics.description: Contritio (repentance) is the interior sorrow and detestation of the committed sin with the purpose of not sinning again; a more perfect contrition (with charity) and imperfect contrition (with other motives) are distinguished and have different effects regarding remission of mortal vs. venial sin (Conc. Trid.; Summa Theol.; Sess. VI, cap. 14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes Tridentine and scholastic treatments: perfect contrition (with charity) remits mortal sin if it includes the resolution and desire for sacramental confession when possible; imperfect contrition suffices for venial sins and disposes to sacramental absolution. Scriptural and patristic citations are provided (Ez. XVIII; Joel II; Luke XIII; Acts II).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Baptism: remission of sins and infusion of sanctifying grace
rubrics_metrics.description: The Council of Trent and the author affirm that baptism remits original and actual sins and infuses virtues and sanctifying grace (though historical theologians debated nuances about 'habit' and 'use').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text records opposing views (some deny infusion of grace in infants) but endorses the Tridentine and majority theological position that baptism, by the efficacy of Christ's death, applies remission and infuses habitual sanctifying grace as to habit if not yet to operative use; references to Conc. Trid. Sess. V & VI and various theologians (Suarez, Vasquez, etc.) are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification includes sanctification and interior renewal, not only forensic remission
rubrics_metrics.description: Sess. VI, cap. 7: 'Iustificatio non est sola peccatorum remissio, sed et sanctificatio et renovatio interioris hominis per voluntariam susceptionem gratiae et donorum.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Council language is used to define justification as a compound reality: forensic declaration, infusion of sanctifying grace, and interior transformation; subsequent canons (e.g., can. 11) anathematize views that would reduce justification to mere imputation without grace and charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental role of baptism and faith in justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Baptism is described as 'sacramentum fidei' and an instrument through which justification is effected; without baptism (and the faith it signifies) justification does not occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Council and scholastics list causes of justification: formal (the justice of God as given), efficient (merciful God), meritorious (Christ's passion), and instrumental (sacrament of baptism and faith). The page cites Sess. VI, cap. 7 and Denzinger-Bannwart numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctifying grace as a habitual, supernatural quality of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: The text treats sanctifying (habitual) grace as a real spiritual quality or 'habit' infused by God in the soul (though some scholastics debate precise metaphysical categorization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations from Summa Theol. and other scholastic sources classify grace as a moral/spiritual quality (De Veritate, Summa) and discuss whether it is a true habit, an accidental property, or a modal accident; the Council's language ('inhaeret') supports permanence/stability as a habit-like quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between efficacious grace and congruous (congrua) grace
rubrics_metrics.description: The text refers to the distinction: efficacious grace infallibly produces its effect in the recipient (when considered physically), whereas congruous grace is that which, in a moral sense or as fitting/preparatory, disposes but does not inexorably determine effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations include Lessius and discussions of 'congrua et efficax' grace; theological debate concerns how to reconcile divine foreknowledge and freedom with efficacious influence. Examples and authorities (Jesuits, Thomists) are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit faith suffices where explicit revelation was not received
rubrics_metrics.description: St. Thomas and others hold that those to whom revelation was not made may be saved by an implicit faith in divine providence (implicitum) and thus may be justified without explicit faith in Christ in the formal sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion distinguishes obligations of those with and without access to revealed proclamation; the page cites Summa Theol. and pastoral implications for heathens (see supra references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith must be accompanied by hope, charity, and works for efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Scriptural and patristic citations (James 2; 1 Cor. 13; Gal. V,6) are used to assert that faith without charity and corresponding works is 'dead' and does not suffice for the life of justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts Reformers' interpretations with the Catholic insistence that faith working through love (fides quae per caritatem operatur) is the living, salvific faith; canons (Conc. Trid. can. 28) condemn assertions that faith without charity is true saving faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of justification as forensic declaration and participation in Christ's righteousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification is defined (Apol. Confess. August.; Solida Declar.) as to pronounce the sinner just and to absolve from sins, by imputation of Christ's righteousness given through faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page collates traditional definitions distinguishing the forensic/declared aspect (pronouncing just) and the real participation (grace infused) — both aspects are affirmed by Trent and the scholastics, with references to Bellarmine and other authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tridentine anathemas and dogmatic prohibitions as doctrinal tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous Tridentine canons are cited (e.g., Sess. VI, can. 9, 10, 11, 12, 24, 28), which pronounce anathema upon particular formulations (e.g., sola fide, denial of infused grace, reduction of faith to mere trust).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These canons function as binding doctrinal criteria: to be orthodox in the Catholic sense one must not hold the condemned propositions. The text repeatedly references Denzinger-Bannwart numbers for these dogmatic statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theological distinctions about the metaphysical status of grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholastic debate enumerated: whether sanctifying grace is a real substantial form, a proper habit, or an accidental/modal quality of the soul (Summa Theol. 1a 2ae and various modern commentators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors cited (Suarez, Billuart, Ripalda, Tepe, Schiffini) argue different metaphysical accounts; the page summarizes positions and notes the Council’s pastoral, not metaphysical, insistence that grace truly 'inhaeret' in the justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility that God may conserve sanctifying grace despite subsequent sin
rubrics_metrics.description: Suarez is quoted to the effect that, notwithstanding opposition and connatural repugnance, God by absolute power could preserve grace in one who has sinned without remitting the sin (i.e., conserve sanctifying grace even with the presence of sin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a theological opinion addressing difficult questions about the loss/preservation of habitual grace after mortal sin; the page cites Suarez and others as part of broader debates.
